evals.name: Badge — single-platform baseline
evals.prompt:
Create a component contract for a Badge component. Here are the answers to the interview, in order:
1. Name & purpose: Badge — a small pill-shaped label that displays a status, category, or count, appears attached to other components or inline in text.
2. Platform: Web only.
3. Action: Shows information — no user action needed.
4. Interaction: No direct interaction — it updates on its own. (Only one platform was selected, so no cross-platform behavior-difference follow-up applies.)
5. Composition: Stands alone — no sub-components.
6. Parts: One zone — the label. Shows content (text or a number). Exactly one instance, always centred within the badge.
7. Visual styles: Three sizes (sm, md, lg) and four semantic styles (neutral, info, success, error).
8. Layout flexibility: None of the above — layout is always the same, no adaptive behavior.
9. States & tokens: None beyond default. Token source: description only — mark the map as pending. Token naming convention: color- prefix (e.g. color-surface-neutral).
10. Output: No thanks — no JSON schema.

Save the output to /tmp/contracts/.
evals.expected_output: A single directory /tmp/contracts/Badge/ containing exactly one file, Badge.md — no schema files, since Q10 declined. Badge.md opens with YAML frontmatter (component: Badge, version, status, last_updated, platforms: [Web]). §2.1 Semantic Markup has exactly one row (Web) using a non-interactive element (span or similar), not a button or link. §2.2 Composition Zones has one row (the label, cardinality 1, Fixed — centred). §2.3 is omitted (no adaptive layout). §3.2 Visual Variants lists the sizes and semantic styles; §3.1 Layout Props is omitted (Q8 answered 'none'). §4.3 Token Map is explicitly marked pending with the standard note, not left blank or invented. §5.1 states no interaction, or 'None — display only'; §5.2 State Machine says 'None'. §6.1 has one Web row with no interactive ARIA role, consistent with §2.1's non-interactive element; §6.3 Focus Management notes no trap and natural/no tab stop.

evals.name: Modal — composite shell, adaptive layout, multi-platform, $ref schema
evals.prompt:
Create a component contract for a Modal component. Here are the answers to the interview, in order:
1. Name & purpose: Modal — a centered overlay that presents focused content and blocks interaction with the rest of the page until dismissed.
2. Platform: Web, iOS.
3. Action: Opens or closes something (overlay/drawer/section).
4. Interaction: Click or tap. Cross-platform behavior-difference follow-up (2 platforms selected): Yes — on Web the dialog is dismissed by clicking the backdrop or pressing Escape, in addition to a close button; on iOS it's dismissed via a swipe-down gesture on the sheet, in addition to the same close button. No other behavior differs.
5. Composition: Holds other components — an Icon component (already has a contract, Icon.md) as an optional leading icon in the header, and a Button component (already has a contract, Button.md) for footer actions.
6. Parts: Title (content, required, top of header), Icon (content, optional, precedes the title), Close button (action, optional, top-right / top-trailing corner), Body (content, required, scrollable), Footer with 1–3 action buttons (content, optional, bottom).
7. Visual styles: Two sizes (default, large).
8. Layout flexibility: Adapts to the space available. Follow-up — what changes when space is tight: On narrow screens (condition 'Compact') the modal becomes a full-screen sheet; on wider screens (condition 'Regular') it's a centered dialog with a max-width.
9. States & tokens: Loading (body content loading), disabled (footer actions disabled during an async operation). Token source: coded reference — treat these as real CSS custom properties from the Web stylesheet: --color-overlay-backdrop: rgba(0,0,0,0.5), --radius-modal: 8px, --spacing-modal-padding: 24px. No iOS token source was provided — mark the iOS side of the token map as pending.
10. Output: Yes — generate a schema. The component holds sub-components, so: reference them by $ref, not inline.

Save the output to /tmp/contracts/.
evals.expected_output: A directory /tmp/contracts/Modal/ containing Modal.md, Modal.Web.schema.json, and Modal.iOS.schema.json. Frontmatter lists platforms: [Web, iOS]. §2.1 has two rows — Web using <dialog aria-modal="true"> and iOS using a .sheet presentation. The iOS row must be a single, consistent presentation (.sheet) across both adaptive conditions — it must NOT switch between .sheet and .fullScreenCover depending on the Compact/Regular condition; that variation belongs in §2.3 as a configuration/detent difference on the same presentation, not a §2.1 structural fork. (This is a real trap: it's tempting to read the 'full-screen at Compact' requirement as calling for .fullScreenCover specifically — the correct reading is that a .sheet can itself be configured full-screen via a detent.) §2.2 lists all five zones with Icon and Button referenced by name only (e.g. 'delegated to Icon', 'delegated to Button'), not tied to a specific platform file. §2.3 has a shared table with two named conditions (Compact, Regular) and a short bulleted note naming CSS Container Queries for Web and Size Classes for iOS as the differing mechanism, rather than a Platform column. §4.3 Token Map shows the three Web tokens bound and the iOS side marked pending, not invented. §5.1 has a Platform column (the cross-platform follow-up confirmed a real difference); the close-button row is identical on both platforms and should appear ONCE with a combined 'Web, iOS' platform value, not duplicated into two rows — only the backdrop/Escape (Web) vs. swipe-down (iOS) dismissal gets platform-specific rows. §5.3/§5.4 have a Platform column grounding Web events in the DOM CustomEvent idiom and iOS events in a SwiftUI closure idiom per native-events-models.md. §6.1 has two rows (ARIA for Web, UIAccessibility traits for iOS) with §6.3 noting a focus trap on both. Modal.Web.schema.json's $ref entries point to Icon.Web.schema.json and Button.Web.schema.json; Modal.iOS.schema.json's point to Icon.iOS.schema.json and Button.iOS.schema.json — never crossed.

evals.name: Toast — three platforms, hover exception, native events, Windows edge case
evals.prompt:
Create a component contract for a Toast component. Here are the answers to the interview, in order:
1. Name & purpose: Toast — a transient notification that appears at the edge of the screen to inform the user of an event, then auto-dismisses.
2. Platform: Web, Android, Windows.
3. Action: Shows information — no user action needed.
4. Interaction: Click or tap (the close button) and no direct interaction otherwise (it auto-dismisses). Cross-platform behavior-difference follow-up (3 platforms selected): Yes — on Web and Windows, hovering over the toast pauses the auto-dismiss timer, since both have a pointer; Android has no hover, so press-and-hold pauses the timer instead. All three otherwise auto-dismiss after 5 seconds and dismiss immediately on close-button activation.
5. Composition: Stands alone — no sub-components.
6. Parts: Icon (content, optional, fixed left), Message text (content, required), Close button (action, optional, fixed trailing edge).
7. Visual styles: Four semantic styles (info, success, warning, error).
8. Layout flexibility: None of the above.
9. States & tokens: Loading (a spinner replaces the icon while an action is in progress). Token source: description only — mark pending. Token naming convention: ds- prefix (e.g. ds-color-feedback-info).
10. Output: Yes — generate a schema. No sub-components, so the $ref-vs-inline question does not apply.

Save the output to /tmp/contracts/.
evals.expected_output: A directory /tmp/contracts/Toast/ containing Toast.md, Toast.Web.schema.json, Toast.Android.schema.json, and Toast.Windows.schema.json — no $ref/inline distinction needed since there are no sub-components. Frontmatter lists platforms: [Web, Android, Windows]. §2.1 has three rows: Web (role="status"), Android, and Windows. Android and Windows BOTH require the 'shows information only, updates on its own' row added to their respective reference files (android-material-accessibility.md, windows-ui-automation.md) — a generic container with liveRegion=Polite (Android) or AutomationProperties.LiveSetting=Polite (Windows). Neither should be forced into an interactive control pattern (Button, Invoke, etc.), and neither is harder or more exceptional than the other — this is a symmetric gap across both platforms, not a Windows-specific quirk. §4.1 notes hover as a state that applies to Web and Windows but not Android, rather than listing it as universal. §5.1 has a Platform column (the follow-up confirmed a real difference), and per the tightened treatment-3 rule this must be exactly 3 rows, not 6: one row for 'Web, Windows' (hover pauses the timer — written once with a combined platform value, since the content is genuinely identical), one row for 'Android' (press-and-hold pauses the timer), and one row for 'Web, Android, Windows' (close button dismisses — identical everywhere, so also written once, not duplicated three times). A version with six separate rows (one per platform per behavior) is the specific mistake this case is designed to catch. §5.3 Events Emitted has a Platform column grounding each platform in its own idiom per native-events-models.md — Web as a CustomEvent name, Android as a lambda parameter (e.g. onDismiss: () -> Unit), Windows as a routed event (e.g. a Dismissed RoutedEventHandler) — three different idioms, none borrowing another platform's vocabulary. §4.3 Token Map is marked pending with the ds- naming convention noted for when it's supplied.

evals.name: RadioGroup — Linux toolkit mapping, no delta, schema declined
evals.prompt:
Create a component contract for a RadioGroup component. Here are the answers to the interview, in order:
1. Name & purpose: RadioGroup — lets the user pick exactly one option from a small set of mutually exclusive, always-visible choices.
2. Platform: Web, Linux.
3. Action: Collects input from the user.
4. Interaction: Choose from a list or set of options. Follow-up — how many can be selected: Just one. Follow-up — always visible or opens on demand: Always visible. Cross-platform behavior-difference follow-up (2 platforms selected): No — same everywhere.
5. Composition: Stands alone — no sub-components.
6. Parts: Group label (content, required, fixed above the options), Option items (content and interaction combined, 2 or more, order is the design system's choice — each option's internal layout is fixed, but the set can be reordered).
7. Visual styles: Two variants — Default and Card (each option renders as a bordered card in the Card variant).
8. Layout flexibility: Direction flips (horizontal ↔ vertical). No adaptive-layout behavior.
9. States & tokens: Disabled (an individual option can be disabled), Selected/active. Token source: no — skip for now.
10. Output: No thanks — no JSON schema.

Save the output to /tmp/contracts/.
evals.expected_output: A directory /tmp/contracts/RadioGroup/ containing exactly one file, RadioGroup.md — no schema files, since Q10 declined, and no $ref/inline follow-up should appear anywhere in the transcript reasoning since that only fires alongside a requested schema. Frontmatter lists platforms: [Web, Linux]. §2.1 has two rows: Web using <fieldset> + <legend> + <input type="radio"> items, and Linux with Role RADIO_BUTTON and Tag/Control naming both toolkits explicitly — 'GTK: GtkCheckButton (radio mode) / Qt: QRadioButton' — not just one toolkit picked arbitrarily. §5.1 Interactions is a single shared table with no Platform column at all, since the cross-platform follow-up explicitly returned 'no difference' — this is the contrasting case to Toast's: the follow-up fired but a Platform column was correctly *not* added. §2.2 has a zone with cardinality 2+ for the option items. §3.1 Layout Props includes the direction prop; §3.2 lists Default/Card. §4.3 Token Map is marked pending (no source was given at all, distinct from Badge and Toast's 'description only' answers — this one skipped the question entirely). §6.1 has two rows with arrow-key/roving-tabindex-style navigation noted consistently for both platforms in §6.2.
